summary.text: Take \(n=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\), where the two odd factors are prime; multiplicativity gives \(\sigma_1(n)=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010=66183576284700\) and \(\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma_1(d)=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011=132367152569399\). Hence \(a(n)=2\sigma_1(n)-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma_1(d)=1\), although \(n\ne1,12\), furnishing a counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e\) denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(m\). The deficiency used in the definition of A296075 is the integer
\[
\delta(m)=2m-\sigma(m),
\]
so that
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) for which this sum is \(1\).

Define
\[
T(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Separating the two terms in the definition of \(a(n)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=2\sum_{d\mid n}d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-T(n). \tag{1}
\end{aligned}
\]
All these equalities are equalities of integers; this matters because individual deficiencies may be negative.

We will use the fact that both \(\sigma\) and \(T\) are multiplicative. For completeness, suppose that \(x\) and \(y\) are coprime. Every divisor of \(xy\) is uniquely of the form \(rs\), where \(r\mid x\) and \(s\mid y\), and \(r,s\) are coprime. The same unique factorization of divisors shows first that
\[
\sigma(xy)=\sum_{r\mid x,\,s\mid y}rs
 =\left(\sum_{r\mid x}r\right)\left(\sum_{s\mid y}s\right)
 =\sigma(x)\sigma(y). \tag{2}
\]
Using this in the definition of \(T\), we likewise obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(xy)
 &=\sum_{d\mid xy}\sigma(d)
 =\sum_{r\mid x,\,s\mid y}\sigma(rs)\\
 &=\sum_{r\mid x,\,s\mid y}\sigma(r)\sigma(s)
 =T(x)T(y). \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus both functions can be evaluated factor by factor on a product of pairwise coprime prime powers.

The counterexample is
\[
N=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009. \tag{4}
\]
We need that \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime. Here is a finite primality certificate, included to make the factorization argument self-contained.

We use the following elementary form of Lucas's primality criterion. Let \(m>1\). Suppose the prime divisors of \(m-1\) are known, and there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m
\]
and, for every prime \(q\mid m-1\),
\[
b^{(m-1)/q}\not\equiv1\pmod m.
\]
Then \(m\) is prime. Indeed, the first congruence makes \(b\) a unit modulo \(m\). Its multiplicative order divides \(m-1\). If that order were a proper divisor of \(m-1\), some prime \(q\mid m-1\) could be removed while retaining divisibility of the order, contrary to the second set of congruences. Hence the order is exactly \(m-1\). It follows that the group of units modulo \(m\) has at least \(m-1\) elements. Since there are only \(m-1\) nonzero residue classes, every nonzero class is a unit, which is possible only when \(m\) is prime.

The following table gives certificates of precisely this kind. In each row, the displayed factorization is the complete factorization of \(m-1\), \(b^{m-1}\) has residue \(1\) modulo \(m\), and the last column lists, for every distinct prime \(q\) in that factorization, the residue of \(b^{(m-1)/q}\) modulo \(m\). None of those listed residues is \(1\). All entries are obtained by ordinary repeated squaring.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 m & m-1 & b & \bigl(q: b^{(m-1)/q}\bmod m\bigr)\\ \hline
 3 & 2 & 2 & 2:2\\
 5 & 2^2 & 2 & 2:4\\
 7 & 2\cdot3 & 3 & 2:6,\ 3:2\\
 19 & 2\cdot3^2 & 2 & 2:18,\ 3:7\\
 29 & 2^2\cdot7 & 2 & 2:28,\ 7:16\\
 229 & 2^2\cdot3\cdot19 & 6 & 2:228,\ 3:134,\ 19:165\\
 57251 & 2\cdot5^3\cdot229 & 2 & 2:57250,\ 5:55371,\ 229:48088\\
 4409 & 2^3\cdot19\cdot29 & 3 & 2:4408,\ 19:209,\ 29:3965\\
 458009 & 2^3\cdot57251 & 3 & 2:458008,\ 57251:6561
\end{array}
\]
Starting from the evident primality of \(2\), the criterion applied successively to the rows proves that \(3,5,7,19,29,229,57251,4409\), and \(458009\) are prime. In particular, the last two numbers are distinct odd primes, so the three factors \(2^{14},4409,458009\) in (4) are pairwise coprime. Direct multiplication also confirms (4):
\[
2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009=33085221781504.
\]

It remains to evaluate \(\sigma\) and \(T\) on these three factors. For a prime \(p\), the divisors of \(p^k\) are \(1,p,\ldots,p^k\), and therefore
\[
\sigma(p^k)=1+p+\cdots+p^k. \tag{5}
\]
For \(2^{14}\), this gives
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767. \tag{6}
\]
For either prime appearing to the first power, (5) gives
\[
\sigma(4409)=4410,\qquad \sigma(458009)=458010. \tag{7}
\]

For \(T(2^{14})\), its divisors are \(2^j\) for \(0\leq j\leq14\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}\sigma(2^j)
 =\sum_{j=0}^{14}(2^{j+1}-1)\\
 &=2(2^{15}-1)-15
 =65534-15
 =65519. \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(p\) is prime, the only divisors of \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), and hence
\[
T(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
T(4409)=4411,\qquad T(458009)=458011. \tag{9}
\]

Applying multiplicativity (2) to the pairwise coprime factorization (4), and using (6) and (7), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(N)
 &=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010\\
 &=144502470\cdot458010\\
 &=66183576284700. \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
Likewise, multiplicativity (3), together with (8) and (9), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(N)
 &=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011\\
 &=289004309\cdot458011\\
 &=132367152569399. \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting (10) and (11) into identity (1), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\sigma(N)-T(N)\\
 &=2\cdot66183576284700-132367152569399\\
 &=132367152569400-132367152569399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
But
\[
N=33085221781504>12,
\]
so \(N\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\). Thus there is a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) whose sum of divisor deficiencies equals \(1\). This counterexample disproves the proposed biconditional that \(a(n)=1\) holds exactly for \(n=1\) or \(n=12\).
